questions.q: Can a permission set remove a permission that a user's profile already grants?
options: Yes, using the Deny checkbox
No -- neither profiles nor permission sets have a deny/remove setting for object or field permissions
Yes, but only for custom fields
Yes, if it's assigned after the profile
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that neither profiles nor permission sets can subtract access — only the absence of any grant results in no access.

questions.q: What controls object and field-level access ('what can this user do')?
options: Organization-wide defaults and the role hierarchy
Profiles, permission sets, and field-level security
Sharing rules and manual sharing
Public groups and queues
questions.explain: Profiles, permission sets, and field-level security answer the 'what can they do' question; OWD, roles, and sharing answer 'which records.'

questions.q: What are the two independent checkboxes FLS sets per field, per profile or permission set?
options: Create Access and Delete Access
View All and Modify All
Read Access and Edit Access
Public Access and Private Access
questions.explain: FLS is set with Read Access and Edit Access as two independent checkboxes per field.

questions.q: How many profiles can a single Salesforce user have?
options: As many as needed, stacked together
Exactly one, assigned at user creation and required
Zero or one, at the admin's discretion
Exactly one per app the user has access to
questions.explain: Every user has exactly one profile, assigned when the user record is created, and it's required.

questions.q: Since Winter '21, what changed about CRUD on standard objects for standard profiles?
options: It was removed from Salesforce entirely
It became editable only through Apex code
Editing it was disabled -- only custom profiles let an admin edit those attributes
It now requires View All to be enabled first
questions.explain: The guide notes that editing standard objects on standard profiles has been disabled since Winter '21; custom profiles remain editable.

questions.q: What role does Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD) play in the record-access stack, per this lesson?
options: It's an optional setting most orgs skip
It's the baseline floor -- every other mechanism only ever widens what OWD allows, never narrows it
It's the final, most restrictive check applied after everything else
It only applies to custom objects, never standard ones
questions.explain: OWD sets the baseline record access, and sharing rules, role hierarchy, and manual sharing can only widen it from there.

questions.q: What two things are set independently per team member when adding them to a team?
options: Their profile and their permission set
Their Team Role and their Access Level on the record
Their organization-wide default and their role hierarchy position
Their login hours and password policy
questions.explain: Each team member gets a free-text Team Role plus an independent Access Level (Read Only or Read/Write).

questions.q: How does an admin or owner actually perform a manual share?
options: By writing a criteria-based sharing rule
By editing the role hierarchy
Through the record's own Share button, granting access to one specific user or group
By changing the object's organization-wide default
questions.explain: Manual sharing happens directly on the record via its Share button, not through any rule or hierarchy setting.

questions.q: Why is turning off Grant Access Using Hierarchies rare?
options: It's disabled by Salesforce for all orgs
It can make a manager genuinely unable to see records through the hierarchy alone, which most orgs don't want
It requires a special license
It only works on custom objects with Master-Detail relationships
questions.explain: Turning it off deliberately breaks the usual assumption that management structure grants visibility — unusual enough that most orgs never touch it.

questions.q: What interaction pattern does adding members to a Queue use, per this lesson?
options: A drag-and-drop canvas unique to queues
The same Available/Selected, Add/Remove picker pattern used for roles, groups, and manual sharing
A criteria-based rule builder
Direct edits to the role hierarchy tree
questions.explain: The lesson notes Queue Members reuses the same picker pattern seen throughout the chapter for granting access to specific users or groups.

questions.q: Why is a criteria-based sharing rule used for national accounts rather than relying on hierarchy?
options: Criteria-based rules are faster to build than hierarchy
National accounts are co-sold across regions, which the hierarchy's chain-of-command shape can't reach
Criteria-based rules replace the need for OWDs
Hierarchy only works for Leads, not Opportunities
questions.explain: National accounts cross regional boundaries, so a criteria-based rule (Account Type = National Account) reaches the co-sell team that hierarchy alone can't.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say View All and Modify All deserve periodic re-justification rather than a one-time grant?
options: Because they bypass restriction rules entirely and are easy to leave in place long after the original reason is gone
Because they expire automatically after 90 days
Because they are disabled by default in every edition
Because only Apex code can grant them
questions.explain: View All/Modify All override restriction-rule narrowing (Lesson 16) and are exactly the kind of broad, easy-to-forget grant an access review should catch.

questions.q: Why does Harbor Point use a case team for escalation instead of simply reassigning the case to Tier 2?
options: Reassignment is not technically possible on Case records
Case teams are required by Salesforce for all support processes
Case teams are faster to configure than reassignment
Reassigning loses the original agent's context; a case team keeps them visible while the new tier takes over ownership
questions.explain: Adding the next tier to the case team (rather than reassigning) preserves the prior agent's access and history instead of erasing it.

questions.q: What does Login As actually do?
options: It opens a real session as another active user, without needing their password, showing exactly what they see
It changes the target user's password so you can log in as them
It simulates access without creating a real session
It only works for inactive users being reactivated
questions.explain: Login As opens a genuine session under the target user's identity — their layouts, access, and UI — and every action in it is logged.

questions.q: What does Finding 2 (three near-identical profiles) recommend, and what pattern does it illustrate?
options: Deleting all three profiles with no replacement
Creating a fourth profile to merge the other three
Consolidating to one profile plus a permission set for the real differences — profile explosion
Converting the profiles into sharing rules
questions.explain: The three profiles differed by only two fields and one tab, so the fix consolidates to a single profile with a permission set carrying the Commercial Lines-specific access — exactly the profile-explosion pattern from Lesson 19.

questions.q: How does this course's scope compare to the Sharing and Visibility Architect specialization mentioned in this lesson?
options: They cover exactly the same material at the same depth
The Architect specialization replaces the need for this course entirely
This course covers correct use of the full toolbox for a typical org; the Architect specialization goes deeper into scale, performance, and defensible design tradeoffs
This course is more advanced than the Architect specialization
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this course is fundamentals-level, while the Architect path goes further into scale (millions of records/users), recalculation performance tuning, and deep territory design.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend granting Create (not Read) on Lead for a public lead-capture form guest profile?
options: Because Read is always required regardless of the form's purpose
Because Create and Read are the same permission in guest profiles
Because Lead records cannot be created by guest users under any configuration
Because the form's actual function only needs Create, and granting Read just because it's convenient to test with adds unnecessary exposure
questions.explain: The lesson's principle is granting only what the site's actual functionality needs — a submission form needs Create, not Read access to existing leads.

questions.q: What distinguishes session security (this lesson) from everything covered in Chapters 1-3?
options: Chapters 1-3 cover what a logged-in user can see and do; session security is about whether the authenticated connection itself is secure
Session security is just another name for field-level security
Session security replaces the need for OWD and sharing rules
There is no meaningful difference
questions.explain: The lesson frames session security as a distinct, underlying layer — independent of what permissions a user holds once authenticated.

questions.q: What does the Sharing Settings page in Setup actually contain?
options: OWD per object, sharing rules, and org-wide toggles like guest user record access, all in one place
Only the org-wide default settings
Only field-level security settings
A list of all users and their passwords
questions.explain: The page is the home for OWD, sharing rules, and several org-wide access toggles — the single screen view of the org's record-access model.
